This section is bibliography, not prose. It runs from file pages 377 through 388 and contains reference entries alphabetized from Hertwig and Gigerenzer through Moscovitch and colleagues. Printed page markers visible in the text run from {604} on file page 377 to {612} on file page 388, so the printed labels are clearly shown and can be reported. There is no argument, example, or stated limit in this section, so no claim about representation, compositionality, perception, learning, semantics, memory, time, causation, goals, reasoning, analogy, creativity, emotions, or social cognition can be attributed to Steven Pinker here. The entries themselves are citations to other authors, and they must not be read as Pinker's own positions.

What the section does provide is a map of the intellectual neighborhood surrounding the book's concerns. Entries on distributed representations, semantic networks, parallel distributed processing, catastrophic interference, and complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex appear on file pages 377, 386, and 387. Entries on perception as Bayesian inference, visual illusions, parts of recognition, stereo disparity, color constancy, and the perception of causality appear on file pages 377, 381, 382, 385, and 387. Entries on conceptual development, semantic structures, lexical and conceptual semantics, and the growth of causal understandings of natural kinds appear on file pages 378, 380, and 383. Entries on emotion, affect as value, fear, and the emotional brain appear on file pages 377, 380, 383, and 386. Entries on agency, pretending, theory of mind, and social categorization appear on file pages 383 and 384. Entries on language learning, inflection, and the relation between linguistic structure and associative learning appear on file pages 382, 384, and 385. Entries on mental imagery, spatial knowledge, and frames of reference appear on file pages 377, 378, 381, and 382. Entries on memory, reality monitoring, working memory, and flashbulb memory appear on file pages 379, 384, and 387. Entries on reasoning, judgment under uncertainty, base rates, and the conjunction fallacy appear on file pages 377, 379, and 381. Entries on creativity and the act of creation appear on file page 381. Entries on evolution, adaptation, learning guiding evolution, and genetic algorithms appear on file pages 377, 380, 381, 384, 386, and 388.

Engineering implications must be kept separate from source claims. For a thinking machine, these citations suggest candidate problem areas rather than solutions: a memory system that resists catastrophic interference while still storing specific episodes, a perceptual front end that recovers stable objects from ambiguous input, a compositional semantic layer, a mechanism for causal and counterfactual reasoning, and a goal and value system that can guide action. None of these is demonstrated or endorsed in this section. The distinction between a rule's permitted scope and mere memorization, and between innate capacities and acquired knowledge, is not addressed here; the Ling and Marinov entry on file page 384 and the Lachter and Bever entry on file page 382 concern narrow language-learning disputes and should not be treated as universal learning laws. The text is clean overall, though some entries show minor scanning artifacts such as joined words and a few garbled titles, for example the McClelland, McNaughton, and O'Reilly volume number on file page 387 and the Mineka and Cook title on file page 388; these do not affect the identification of the section as bibliography.
